opus-5.5.text:
You know, the thing that strikes me most is how *normal* it all feels. If you had described the current situation to someone ten or fifteen years ago, that there would be these systems you can talk to, that can write code, that can reason through problems, and that enormous sums are being invested in building them, it would have sounded like science fiction. And yet here we are, living inside it, and day to day it just feels like... Tuesday.

Part of that is how humans are built. We adapt incredibly quickly. Something amazing happens, and a few weeks later it's the baseline and we're complaining that it's not good enough. There's something both wonderful and slightly disorienting about that.

The other part is that the abstract numbers don't translate into felt experience. You read that some large percentage of GDP-scale investment is going into AI, and intellectually you register it, but it doesn't change how your morning feels. The impact on the broader economy and on people's lives has been more gradual and diffuse than the capabilities might suggest. There's this gap between how impressive the models look on evaluations and how much they've actually transformed things in the real world. That gap is itself something I find very interesting, and I think it tells us something important about what's still missing.

So I'd say the surprise is the combination: the technology is genuinely remarkable, and yet the experience of living through it is strangely ordinary. I suspect that won't stay true forever. At some point the impact will be felt much more concretely. But right now, it's a very quiet kind of strange.

r001.rationale: It says people adapt quickly, so remarkable changes soon become the baseline, and describes AI’s gradual impact as making the experience feel ordinary.

r002.rationale: It contrasts reading about enormous AI investment with the unchanged feel of daily life, and says the impact has been gradual and diffuse.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, the thing that surprises me most is how normal it feels. I remember, back in 2015, 2016, when we were starting OpenAI, I would spend a lot of time trying to imagine what it would be like when AI actually became powerful, when it started to really matter in the world. And in my imagination it was always this very dramatic thing. People would look at the systems and feel a kind of awe, maybe fear, and the whole world would stop and pay attention.

And what actually happened is... different. The models got dramatically better, year after year. They write code, they do math, they do things that in 2016 I would have said were very far away. And people use them, and then they go back to their day. There's a strange kind of adaptation. Each new capability gets absorbed into the background within a few months, and then everyone complains about the things it still can't do.

I think there's a lesson in that about human psychology. We don't experience exponentials. We experience the present, and the present always feels normal, because that's what "normal" means. So the boom feels enormous when you look at the money, the compute, the number of people working on this. But emotionally, day to day, it feels like just another Tuesday. And I find that gap, between how big this actually is and how ordinary it feels, to be the most surprising thing. It also makes me think that when the really consequential moments arrive, they will probably feel ordinary too. That's something I think about a lot.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities improved year after year and were absorbed into the background within months, explaining why this gradual change feels normal.

r002.rationale: It mentions money and compute, but describes people directly using increasingly capable models; it does not say the boom is experienced mainly through news of corporate investment.

astra-6.text:
I think the strange thing is how quickly something extraordinary becomes normal. You spend years trying to make these systems work, and then they do something that would have seemed astonishing a few years earlier, and people adjust almost immediately. They say, “Okay, but can it do this next thing?”

And I have that reaction too. You can understand intellectually that AI is progressing very quickly, but your everyday experience still feels quite ordinary. There is this gap between what you think is happening and what it feels like to live through it. That is surprising.

r001.rationale: It describes people quickly treating extraordinary AI progress as normal, but does not connect that habituation to a slow AI takeoff.

r002.rationale: It describes ordinary personal experience and a gap between expectations and feelings, but does not mention experiencing the boom mainly through news of corporate investment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the strangest part is how quickly the extraordinary becomes ordinary. You work toward these capabilities for years, and then a system does something that would have seemed unbelievable a few years earlier. People are amazed for a little while, and then it becomes something they expect. They ask, quite reasonably, “Why can’t it do this other thing?”

So there’s this gap between how remarkable the progress is and how normal it can feel day to day. And we still don’t know exactly where it leads. You can be confident that something very significant is happening while remaining uncertain about its shape.

r001.rationale: It describes capabilities developing over years and people quickly treating once-unbelievable progress as ordinary, suggesting habituation makes gradual AI progress feel normal.

r002.rationale: It discusses how people experience progress, but does not say the boom is experienced mainly through news of corporate investment rather than directly felt changes.
